item.title: Identity Domain
item.description: What is an identity domain? An identity domain (idd) is an explicit namespace for a principal. Two users named user1 can belong to different domains. The string is supplied by trusted integration code or a configured token asserter; it is not proof of authentication. Speedle does not infer or validate a provider’s tenant model merely from the domain name. Represent domains in policies and requests grant user user1 from github read book grant user user1 from IDCS.

item.title: Integrations
item.description: Speedle makes authorization decisions. A policy enforcement point (PEP) in your application, gateway or platform calls Speedle for each decision and enforces the result. The interfaces below are supported today. REST and gRPC APIs Manage services, policies and roles through the Policy Management Service (PMS), and request runtime decisions from the Authorization Decision Service (ADS). Both expose REST APIs; start either server with --grpc-endpoint to enable its gRPC API.

item.title: Logging Framework
item.description: Overview For the release after v1.8.0, Speedle uses Go log/slog for structured application and audit logs and gopkg.in/natefinch/lumberjack.v2 for file rotation. v1.8.0 and older releases use the previous logging API. Logging configuration All existing --log-* and --auditlog-* flags, SPDL_* environment variables and JSON configuration keys remain supported. Explicit flags override environment variables, which override the configuration file. Application defaults are info, text, stderr and no caller metadata; audit defaults are info and JSON.

item.title: Policy Discovery
item.description: Speedle can be used for authorization decisions in systems with a large number of protected resources. Before those protected resources can be accessed, the Speedle authorization decision API (is-allowed API) is called. Defining the authorization policies for those protected resources is difficult if you don't know what actions are occuring on the protected resources, or how a protected resource is expressed in an authorization decision request. Policy discovery mode can make this task much easier

item.title: Security
item.description: Protect both API transports Speedle’s standalone PMS and ADS expose REST and gRPC. Both now use the same --insecure, --cert, --key, --client-cert and --force-client-cert transport settings. Invalid certificates or trust configuration cause startup to fail; secure mode does not fall back to plaintext. TLS encrypts the connection and authenticates the server. To require authenticated clients, provide a client CA with --client-cert and set --force-client-cert=true. Without that flag, a configured CA validates a client certificate only when the client supplies one.

item.title: Speedle Cloud
item.description: Speedle Cloud is a hosted authorization service built on the open-source Speedle engine. Manage services, SPDL authorization and role policies, test decisions in the Playground and call the API from your server. Policy synchronization from Speedle Cloud uses Speedle Cloud ADS: the speedle-cloud binary and image. The self-hosted Speedle Engine speedle-ads binary no longer provides a policy-source store. Speedle Cloud is in public beta. This guide describes the workflow for the live service.

item.title: Speedle Cloud API keys
item.description: API keys belong to your account and can access its services according to their scope. They authenticate your application, not its end users. Managing API keys, sessions and linked identities always requires a signed-in console session. Speedle Cloud is in public beta. This guide describes the workflow for the live service. Create an API key Open API keys, enter a name of 1–128 characters after trimming whitespace, select a scope and an expiry (7d, 30d, 90d, 180d or 365d; the console defaults to 3 months), and choose Create.
